analysis.one_liner: Tightens mine dust limits, speeds black lung benefits, and helps sick miners pay lawyers.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate health committee: introduced July 31, 2013, referred to committee, and it died there when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would protect coal miners from black lung disease in several ways. It orders the Labor Department to issue a final rule lowering the amount of coal and silica dust miners can legally breathe on the job, and to update that rule every five years unless the disease declines. It requires mine operators to give miners a full copy of their own medical exam reports within 14 days, pays lawyers up to $4,500 for miners who win contested benefit claims that drag on too long, and guarantees survivor benefits for widows and children in a set of older and pending claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners exposed to respirable dust, miners and widows with pending or long-pending black lung claims, and lawyers representing claimants whose cases stretch past a year.

how_it_helps.text: Orders a final regulation lowering miners' permissible exposure to respirable coal and silica dust through engineering controls, with mandatory reexamination every five years unless black lung disease declines [S2][S3].
Requires mine operators to deliver a complete copy of an examining physician's report to a miner within 14 days of an examination, so claimants can see the evidence used against them [S2][S3].

Creates an attorneys' fee program, paid from the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, of up to $1,500 per stage and $4,500 total for claimants who prevail in contested claims still unresolved a year after filing, with operators reimbursing the fund when compensation is ultimately ordered [S2][S3].

Restores or guarantees survivors' benefits for widows and children, including claims filed before 1982 and claims pending on or after March 23, 2010, where the miner was entitled to lifetime benefits at death [S2][S3].

Directs the GAO to study barriers to health care for people with black lung disease, especially in rural areas, and directs the Labor Department to review and reduce paperwork barriers in the claims process [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators, who would face stricter dust controls, quicker medical record disclosure, and reimbursement of claimants' legal fees in cases they ultimately lose; the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund front-pays some legal fees until operators reimburse it.

drawbacks.text: Stricter respirable dust limits would require mine operators to invest in ventilation and dust-control engineering, which the industry has historically argued is costly and, in some seams, technically difficult; those costs fall on operators and potentially on production [S3].

The legal-fee program draws initially on the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, shifting front-end administrative costs onto a fund financed by coal excise taxes until operators reimburse it in cases where compensation is ordered [S3].

Codifying an aggressive exposure-reduction standard in statute, with a six-month deadline for a final rule, gives the agency little time for the technical sampling and feasibility work normally done through notice-and-comment rulemaking [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits — lower dust exposure, timely access to medical reports, fee support in drawn-out claims, and survivor benefits — fall on a workforce with one of the most clearly documented occupational diseases in the country. The costs are real but bounded: dust-control investment and fee reimbursements for operators. The bill is weighted toward miners' health and benefit access, and its main design weakness is procedural (a very short rulemaking deadline), not substantive.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, so it died at the end of the 113th Congress without a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV introduced the Black Lung Health Improvements Act of 2013 on July 31, 2013, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and PENSIONS the same day [S1][S5].
One Democratic senator cosponsored the bill; no further action was taken after the referral [S4][S5].
No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote appears in the action history, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, without the bill advancing [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators avoided the stricter dust limits, disclosure requirement, and fee reimbursements; miners with black lung disease got no new protection.

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, a package of dust limits, disclosure rules, legal fees, and survivor benefits for coal miners

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Tom Harkin
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote after referral, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor and never reached a vote, so no roll call shows how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill would force operators to cut miners' respirable dust exposure, hand over complete medical exam reports within 14 days, and reimburse the trust fund for claimants' legal fees in cases they lose. These are direct compliance and litigation costs tied to a disease the operators' workplaces cause.

The fund would front-pay attorneys' fees for claimants in qualifying contested claims, adding short-term outlays, but operators must reimburse it when compensation is ordered. The fund exists to pay benefits to disabled miners, so its role expands alongside miners' interests.

industries.industry: Claimant-side attorneys and legal aid for miners
industries.note: The bill creates a fee program paying up to $4,500 per qualifying claim that drags past a year, making it economically viable for lawyers to take contested black lung cases for sick miners.
